entry.title: Corrections: AQI bands in the air report, missing satellite days, and the 24-hour comparison
entry.content:
An audit of our own numbers found several mistakes, now fixed. The Lahore and Islamabad air report converted PM2.5 to US AQI with the pre-2024 EPA breakpoints while saying it used the 2024 ones; every polluted month's AQI was too low (November 2024 in Lahore is 422, not 336) and two Lahore months move up a band. A few hand-typed comparisons in that report were also wrong or unsupported and have been corrected or removed.

NASA's Suomi NPP satellite returned no data on 4–6 November 2024 and missed its afternoon pass on four other season days. The Two Punjabs report, Fire trends and the daily and district pages now say so, treat those days as missing rather than zero where they compare years, and the report's busiest-week table is computed over calendar days (in 2024 both Punjabs peaked in the same week, not two weeks apart as we said). India's official 2025 count is now sourced to The Tribune's season-end figure, 5,085.

On the live map, the "on the 24 h before" comparison now cuts both windows from the same data so they line up; it had been comparing NASA's 24-hour file with a differently timed window. In the daily archive before 17 October, every MODIS detection was labelled Terra, including Aqua's; the files have been regenerated.

entry.title: A page for every day of fires, and for every district
entry.content:
Daily fires now has a page for each day: how many fire spots the satellites saw in Pakistan and India, the change on the day before, the busiest districts and villages, the same date in every year since 2019, and a map. Fires by district gives each district with frequent fires its own page, comparing this season with the same dates in past years.

We also now drop a kind of false alarm: over the Thar desert, a single afternoon pass sometimes flags hundreds of "fires" on hot sand that the other satellites, crossing within the hour, don't see. On 22 October this put Bikaner at the top of the list. Such bursts are now left out of the map and the archive. Past totals for Rajasthan fall, and both Punjabs are unchanged.

entry.title: Report: Two Punjabs, seven seasons of crop fires
entry.content: Our new report, Two Punjabs, counts the crop fires NASA's Suomi NPP satellite saw on both sides of the border every October and November since 2019, the same way on both sides. Indian Punjab's count fell 95% from 2021 to 2025; Pakistani Punjab's didn't fall, and since 2024 it has been higher. Our Indian numbers match India's official counts closely (correlation 0.99). The report also explains why fire counts now undercount Indian burning, and finds no sign of the same shift on the Pakistani side. All reports are now listed under Reports.

entry.title: Fire trends: every burning season since 2019
entry.content: A new page, Fire trends, compares every October–November burning season since 2019 using NASA's archive: daily fires for each season, this year against the same dates in earlier years, where in the two Punjabs the fires are day by day (press play to watch a season), and how many fires the satellite catches at night. Fire counts have fallen by about two-thirds since 2021, but the share seen on the 1:30 am pass has roughly tripled, which suggests some burning has moved to the evening, when no satellite is overhead. Filter any chart by Pakistan or India.

entry.title: Are fires rising? A daily trend, and a daily archive
entry.content: Under the fire count there is now a small bar for each day and a line comparing the last 24 hours with the 24 hours before (for example "↑ 55% on the 24 h before"). It follows the Pakistan and India filters. We also now keep every day's fires, starting from 14 October 2026, so we can later show how burning moves across districts, dates, and day and night passes. Satellites can't see fires through cloud or thick smoke, so single days swing. Daily totals are open at /api/days.

entry.title: Wind on the map: where the air is coming from
entry.content: A new "Wind right now" layer shows ink streaks drifting the way the wind is blowing across the plains, from weather-model winds refreshed every half hour (Open-Meteo). Under "Your air" the site now also says which way the wind is blowing where you are, and which big towns it is coming from and heading towards, so you can see whether smoke from fires upwind is likely to reach you.

entry.title: The whole map in Google Earth
entry.content: You can now open HamariHawa in Google Earth: hamarihawa.org/hamarihawa.kml. It has the same layers as the site, each refreshing on its own schedule: fires in the last 24 hours (every 15 minutes) and 7 days, air quality now in 17 cities, traffic and industry NO₂ hotspots, haze and the daily satellite photo, and the pollution sites. It is a standard KML file, so it also opens in QGIS, ArcGIS and Civil 3D. How to use it.

entry.title: Major roads under the traffic NO₂ layer
entry.content: The traffic and industry NO₂ layer now shows motorways and highways from OpenStreetMap underneath it, with main roads added as you zoom in. They are there for context: the satellite sees NO₂ in squares about 5 km wide, so it shows a city's traffic as one hotspot and can't pick out single roads. Thanks to a reader on Reddit for pushing on this. See Lahore.

entry.title: Traffic is now listed as a pollution source
entry.content: Transport is the biggest source of PM2.5 emitted in Lahore (35%) and Islamabad–Rawalpindi (53%), according to PAQI 2025, but our map only showed it as a layer option. "Traffic exhaust (NO₂ hotspots)" is now the first entry in the map's Pollution sources list, with the number of hotspots and the dates they cover.

entry.title: Every source layer now says when its data is from
entry.content: Fires are live, but the pollution sources are not, so each one now carries its date: methane and CO₂ plumes seen 2022 to September 2026 (Carbon Mapper), brick kilns from satellite surveys published in 2024–2025, always-hot spots from NASA's 2025 fire archive, and landfills, industrial areas and power plants from OpenStreetMap as of 17 October 2026.

entry.title: HamariHawa is live
entry.content: A free live map of what satellites see in the air over Pakistan and North India, in English, Urdu and Hindi. It shows every fire NASA's satellites detect, named after the nearest village; smoke, haze and traffic NO₂; known pollution sources such as 50,000 brick kilns, landfills, power plants and methane plumes; and what the air means for health in 17 cities. There is also a Pollution sites page and a share card for WhatsApp, Instagram, X and Facebook.
